Manthan Fabricare Systems: Who Gets a Salesperson?

A case on product-qualified accounts in laundry and dry-cleaning software

1. Opening

At twenty to eight on Monday morning, 5 October 2026, Aditi Urs stood in the packing hall of a dry-cleaning outlet on Sayyaji Rao Road in Mysuru and watched a counter clerk key three sherwanis into a tablet. The tablet ran Manthan Counter, the free order-management product her company gave away to single-outlet laundries. The owner had just opened a second outlet in Mandya and wanted to link the two.

Aditi, Chief Product Officer of Manthan Fabricare Systems, had a deadline. By Friday 9 October she had to tell the sales and data teams which free accounts should be handed to a salesperson, and on what evidence. The wedding and Diwali season would arrive in early November, when every outlet in the country is at its busiest and a sales call is least welcome.

2. Company background

Manthan Fabricare Systems was founded in Mysuru in 2017. It sells cloud software to laundry and dry-cleaning businesses: order intake, garment tagging, pickup and delivery slots, WhatsApp status messages to customers, UPI QR collection through Razorpay, and GST-ready invoices. Its rivals are mostly not other specialists. They are Tally and Zoho Books for billing, Vyapar for small-shop invoicing, paper tags, and the in-house systems that larger chains such as Tumbledry and UClean have built for themselves.

The company grew the way Zoho, Freshworks and Postman did, by letting the product recruit customers. Manthan Counter is free for one outlet up to 300 orders a month. Manthan Chain, the paid plan, adds multi-outlet reporting, staff roles, higher message limits and integrations. Four salespeople answered demo requests in the order they arrived, and a customer who never asked never heard from anyone.

3. The situation

Neha Devegowda, the company’s data scientist in Toronto, had spent August rebuilding the funnel from raw usage logs. Exhibit 1 shows the six months from April to September 2026. Of 18,000 sign-ups, 7,200 (40 per cent) logged ten or more orders in their first 30 days and counted as activated. Of those, 4,320 (60 per cent) were still active at day 90, and 648 (15 per cent of the active base) had bought Manthan Chain. Overall, 3.6 per cent of sign-ups paid.

The more useful finding came when Neha split the 4,320 active accounts by how they used the product. Exhibit 2 groups them into three segments. Segment A accounts had three or more linked outlets and three or more staff logins. Segment B had two outlets or two or more logins, or had run into the free plan’s order or message limit. Segment C was the single counter. Segment A was only 560 accounts, 13 per cent of the active base, yet it converted at 35 per cent and produced ₹352.8 lakh of first-year contract value, 65 per cent of the ₹540.0 lakh total.

Neha then ran a small pilot in August. She took 120 Segment A accounts, had a rep call them within a fortnight of the second staff login, and held back 120 comparable accounts as a control. Of the called accounts, 60 bought (50 per cent); of the control, 42 did (35 per cent). In Segment B, 100 called accounts produced 25 buyers (25 per cent) against 20 of 100 (20 per cent) untouched. A call added fifteen points in Segment A and five in Segment B.

The team saw it differently depending on where it sat. In New Jersey, Tarun Kempegowda carried a quarterly target and saw 4,320 warm accounts going uncalled. In Singapore, Anand Channegowda’s support queue was already long, and he had watched free users go quiet after an over-eager call. A Dubai laundry group with 41 outlets was trialling Manthan Counter and had asked for a contract. Neha’s signals were counts of outlets, logins and limit-hits, never laundry customers’ phone numbers, in keeping with the DPDP Act.

4. The people

Tarun Kempegowda, Vice President of Sales, works from New Jersey and is responsible for the Gulf and North American chains. He wants every account that looks larger than a single counter routed to sales, and he wants headcount to match.

Harish Puttaswamy, regional sales lead in Hassan, knows the Karnataka chain owners personally. He wants reps to call whoever “looks like a chain” and trusts his eye over a threshold.

Anand Channegowda, customer-success lead in Singapore, wants unsolicited calls kept to a minimum, protects the support queue, and would rather invest in in-product prompts and onboarding.

Neha Devegowda, data scientist in Toronto, wants a written rule that can be measured and revised, and she wants the pilot repeated on a larger sample before anyone spends real money.

5. What a rep costs

A fully loaded salesperson costs Manthan ₹18 lakh a year, or ₹9 lakh for the six months the plan covers. In that time a rep can work about 140 accounts properly: a discovery call, a demo for the owner and a follow-up. Four reps therefore work 560 accounts, exactly the size of Segment A, at a cost of ₹36 lakh, or about ₹6,400 per account worked. The pilot lifts give the return. A call in Segment A adds fifteen points at ₹1.8 lakh, worth ₹27,000 of first-year value per account called. In Segment B the same call adds five points at ₹0.6 lakh, worth ₹3,000 per account called.

Aditi had three ways forward, compared in Exhibit 3. Each assumes the next six months repeat the mix in Exhibit 2.

6. The options

Option 1: route every Segment A and B account to sales. Tarun’s preference. It reaches all 1,820 accounts and adds the most first-year value, ₹189.0 lakh. But 1,820 accounts at 140 per rep needs 13 reps, nine more than today, costing ₹117.0 lakh for six months. The extra nine reps cost ₹81.0 lakh and add only ₹37.8 lakh, the value of Segment B’s 63 extra buyers.

Option 2: route only Segment A, the accounts with both signals. The four existing reps cover the 560 accounts, add 84 buyers and ₹151.2 lakh, and net ₹115.2 lakh. The cost is that 1,260 growing accounts get no human contact and some of them will be lost, and the threshold rests on a 240-account Segment A arm.

Option 3: stay self-serve and invest in the product. Anand’s preference. It costs nothing in sales time and protects the support queue, but it leaves the fifteen-point lift on the table.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 tell you about where Manthan’s revenue actually comes from, and what would change if you sorted accounts by sign-up date rather than by usage?
  2. Why is the value per account called (₹27,000 against ₹3,000) more useful than the paid rate alone in deciding whom to call?
  3. Compare Options 1 and 2 in Exhibit 3. What is the cost of the nine extra reps, and what does it buy?
  4. Which risks in the pilot would you want to reduce before the rule is made permanent, and how would you monitor them during the festive season?

8. A note for the learner

Product-led sales sits on top of product-led growth. The product does the recruiting and teaching, and usage tells the company which accounts have grown into needs that a person can serve. A product-qualified account is not an account that looks large; it is one whose behaviour shows both fit and depth. The decision turns on whether the value of a call exceeds the cost of the person’s time.

A well-reasoned answer works from the exhibits. Segment A repays a call handsomely, at ₹27,000 of value against about ₹6,400 of cost. Segment B does not, at ₹3,000 against the same cost. Option 1 nets ₹72.0 lakh, Option 2 nets ₹115.2 lakh, and the ₹43.2 lakh difference is the price of calling the wrong accounts.

The defensible path is Option 2 with two additions. Aditi should write the rule down (three or more linked outlets and three or more staff logins, call within 14 days, timed to a limit-hit) so it can be audited. She should also ask Anand to build in-product prompts for Segment B, capturing part of Option 3 at little cost. The Dubai group should be routed as a Segment A account immediately. Neha should extend the control group through the festive season and report after eight weeks, because a 240-account Segment A arm supports a decision but does not settle it. If the fifteen-point lift falls materially, the threshold should be revisited. Finally, the signals should stay counts of outlets, logins and limits, never customers’ personal data, which keeps the programme consistent with the DPDP Act.

Anubhav Loom Networks: What the Score Is Counting

A case on product-qualified accounts in handloom and handicraft export software

1. Sunday night, Cuttack

By nine on the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, the Durga Puja pandals were going up across Balu Bazar, and the hammering carried to the second-floor office on Link Road where Debasmita Mohapatra was still working. In eighteen hours the vice-president of product at Anubhav Loom Networks had to tell a board committee which free accounts her company would put a salesperson in front of, and why.

The call was at half past six on Monday evening, timed so that Dibyajyoti Rout could join from Toronto at nine in the morning and Rudra Praharaj from Berlin at three. On the table was Kalyani Jena's request for nine more inside-sales staff and a field seller in Europe: ₹1.72 crore a year against an annual recurring revenue of ₹9.20 crore. Behind it lay a four-month pilot that appeared to show that a call placed soon after a free account hit a plan limit nearly doubled the chance it would pay.

She had read the pilot four times that weekend, and each reading had made her less certain. The lift was large in one segment and absent in another; the randomisation had held on paper and not in practice; and the measure everyone wanted to make permanent had been fitted on the months it was meant to predict. Beneath that sat a smaller worry: that the signal the company had learned to read was not a signal about its customers at all.

2. The company, and a promise made in 2022

Anubhav Loom Networks was founded in Cuttack in 2019 by Rohit Patnaik, who had spent nine years in his family's merchant-export business shipping Sambalpuri ikat and Pipili appliqué to European wholesalers. The product solved the paperwork of that trade: an order book shared with the buyer, weaver-wise allocation, loom-stage tracking, packing lists, invoice and shipping-bill drafts, and a buyer portal where a European sourcing manager could watch goods move on the loom. It sits alongside Tally and Zoho Books rather than replacing them.

The free plan was set in 2022, and that decision still governs everything. A state cluster-development programme wanted registered weaver co-operatives put on digital order books; Anubhav won the implementation work, took ₹2.60 crore in fees over three years, and promised in exchange a free tier for scheme-registered co-operatives until 31 March 2028. To make the tier useful it was made generous: fifty orders in any rolling thirty days, three logins, unlimited buyer-portal invitations. Two thousand co-operative accounts arrived within eighteen months. Almost none paid, and none can now be gated.

3. The trade the product sits in

India's handloom and handicraft exports move through a chain rather than a firm. A European buyer places an order with a merchant exporter; the merchant exporter distributes it across master weavers and co-operatives in Nuapatna, Bargarh and the Pipili belt; the goods come back, are inspected and shipped against a single shipping bill filed on ICEGATE, with the foreign exchange tracked in the Reserve Bank of India's EDPMS until an electronic bank realisation certificate closes it.

The demand calendar belongs to the buyer. European home-textile ranges are decided in January at Heimtextil in Frankfurt, and Christmas programmes must leave Indian ports by the end of September, which puts the weaving load into May, June and July. None of that is set by the Indian supplier, and none of it says anything about a supplier's willingness to buy software.

The competition is only partly software: larger exporters keep their order books in Excel, and ONDC has made some artisan units curious about selling at home. Freshworks and Zoho are what everyone cites when they say Indian software can be sold without a sales force. Anubhav's own advantage is the buyer portal — once a European sourcing manager watches an order through it, the supplier's choice of software is not entirely the supplier's.

4. The pilot, and what it has since turned out to mean

The plan drawn up in March 2026 was clean. Any free account crossing a plan limit — the fiftieth order in thirty days, a fourth login, an attempt to generate a locked export document — entered a pool and was randomly assigned either to a call from the Berhampur desk within twenty-four hours or to a holdout left alone. Between 1 April and 31 July the pool took in 1,504 accounts, 752 in each arm; conversion meant a paid subscription within sixty days.

This is the exhibit Kalyani has circulated since August, and read alone it is persuasive. Exhibit 3 is the one that has not travelled. Of the 752 accounts assigned to be called, the desk reached 470, which is 62.5 per cent; the rest were never dialled or were dialled once and abandoned.

The arithmetic is uncomfortable. Comparing the 470 reached accounts with the 752 holdout accounts gives a gap of 9.9 points, and that is the figure on Kalyani's slide. But the accounts the reps declined to dial converted at 4.6 per cent, below the 7.3 per cent of the untouched holdout: they were skipping accounts they judged hopeless, and those accounts were indeed hopeless. The honest comparison is the 5.2 points between the assigned arm and the holdout. Nearly half the apparent effect of the call is the effect of the rep's judgement about whom to call — the judgement the score was meant to replace.

Figure 1 is the exhibit Debasmita cannot argue away. Both peaks belong to the buyer's calendar, not the supplier's growth. A co-operative in Bargarh crosses fifty orders in June because a merchant exporter in Cuttack has pushed a Christmas programme down to it. The co-operative has not grown; it has been handed work whose margin belongs to somebody else.

Two further facts emerged in September, after the pilot closed. The first is marked in Figure 1: on 12 June the growth team cut the free order cap from fifty to thirty, hoping to force conversions before the festive season, and nobody told the pilot. The second is Dibyajyoti's: 617 of the 1,504 pooled accounts, 41 per cent, had invited a buyer domain that another pooled account had also invited in the same window. One order moving down the chain was generating limit-hits in two or three accounts at once, each counted as a separate qualified opportunity.

Exhibit 4 is where the average dissolves. In segments E and M a call is worth fifteen and thirteen points; in C and A it is worth under three, and those two were 1,129 of the 1,504 pooled accounts, 75 per cent of everything the trigger produced. Qualifying by limit-hits spends three quarters of the desk's time where calling barely matters — and, because of the 2022 promise, on accounts that cannot be charged anyway.

Exhibit 5 says that when the threshold was made easier to cross, the accounts crossing it became worth less: the lift fell from 6.1 points to 4.0, a third of it gone in seven weeks. The trigger was never a property of the accounts. It was a property of the pricing page, which is edited by a team that does not attend the pilot review.

5. The score

Dibyajyoti's answer, built in September, was to stop using a single limit and to score accounts continuously. The Anubhav Readiness Score gives an account up to a hundred points across six behaviours, and a threshold of 62 marks it a product-qualified account.

Read forwards, Exhibit 7 is a good result: calling only the high-scoring accounts would reach 289 of the 752 assigned and still capture about twenty-three of the thirty-nine additional conversions. Read against Exhibit 4 it is less impressive. Of the 188 accounts from segments E and M in the called arm, 171 cleared the threshold, while only 118 of the 564 accounts from segments C and A did, and inside C and A the score adds almost nothing — its high scorers converted at 5.9 per cent against a base of about four. The score largely reproduces a field the sign-up form already collects free.

6. The people

Debasmita Mohapatra, vice-president of product, Cuttack, owns the rule and the activation numbers she is judged on. She believes the account is the wrong unit of analysis, and has not said so to the board because saying it postpones a decision the board has waited two quarters for.

Rohit Patnaik, chief executive, Cuttack, wants a company that looks like the product-led Indian software firms investors admire, and has told his Series A investor that revenue would come without a sales organisation. He expects to need one, and would rather it arrived called something else.

Kalyani Jena, head of revenue, Cuttack, carries the ₹15 crore target and is paid on bookings; her reps also earn credit per qualified account worked, which is why the disposition codes are the weakest data in the company. She has not volunteered that her two best reps re-sorted their assigned lists by hand.

Dibyajyoti Rout, head of data, Toronto, built the score and wants it adopted because it makes his work legible. He knows it was fitted and tested on the same four months, and that asking for a clean quarter would cost him the decision.

Ranjita Behera, customer-success lead, Balasore, argues that onboarding rather than calling produces paying accounts, and Exhibit 6 supports her. Her budget grows if prompts beat reps. She does not mention that her team books sessions with accounts that already look promising.

Rudra Praharaj, Europe lead, Berlin, thinks the debate provincial and wants to sell to buyers, on the argument that one Malmö sourcing manager can bring fourteen Odisha units onto the platform in a fortnight. His role becomes strategic if that is the plan, and he costs thirteen Berhampur reps.

Khirod Senapati, chief financial officer, Cuttack, says an incremental conversion cannot be invoiced and wants the programme judged on cash collected. He is quietly preparing the case for renegotiating the 2022 co-operative promise.

Rashmi Satpathy, external counsel in Cuttack, notes that the notice in force since 2021 permits contact details to be used "to operate the service and to inform you about its features", and that a call generated by profiling usage may not sit inside that purpose under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. For co-operative accounts the contacts were collected by the cluster programme, not by Anubhav. She declines to put a number on the risk.

7. Voices

"Seventeen point two against seven point three. That is the whole argument. Give me nine people and I will give you the March number."

Kalyani Jena, revenue review, 24 September

"Seventeen point two is the rate among accounts your reps chose to ring. The ones they didn't ring converted at 4.6, which is below the holdout. You are measuring their taste. Their taste is worth something, but it isn't the call."

Dibyajyoti Rout, same meeting, from Toronto

"Every one of you is looking at the supplier. Margit Ekelund placed orders with fourteen units last season. If she asks them to use Anubhav, they use Anubhav. Why are we scoring weavers?"

Rudra Praharaj, chat thread, 2 October

"Because in March we promised the board a repeatable motion, and 'a buyer liked us' is not repeatable. Also, she has asked for one portal across all fourteen. If she gets it, thirteen of our accounts stop generating any signal at all."

Debasmita Mohapatra, same thread

"I can run the calling programme on the present notice if the calls concern features the account has tried to use. A score that ranks customers by how likely they are to spend is a different purpose, and I would want it in a fresh notice with consent taken again."

Rashmi Satpathy, advice note, 6 October

8. The options as Debasmita sees them

The first is Dibyajyoti's score: adopt 62 as the threshold, hold the desk at five, and call about 136 accounts a month against a desk capacity of roughly 118. It is cheap, written down and auditable. It also encodes a segment split the company already knows, and it was fitted on the months it is tested against.

The second is Kalyani's: call every limit-hit and hire the nine. At a mean of 351.9 limit-hits a month the desk must more than double, at ₹70.20 lakh a year for the inside-sales staff. Exhibits 4 and 5 argue against it; Exhibit 2, the only one the board has seen, argues for it.

The third is Ranjita's: no outbound programme, and money into in-product prompts and onboarding instead. It is the cheapest and it fits the story Rohit has told investors. It also makes the score unusable, since two-fifths of it is generated by the onboarding it would expand.

The fourth is Rudra's: put the seller in Europe and sell to buyers, so that supplier adoption follows the buyer's choice. One seller at ₹101.76 lakh costs as much as thirteen Berhampur reps, and there are no exhibits at all about buyers.

Underneath all four sits the assumption Debasmita keeps returning to: that the account is the thing to qualify. Exhibit 1 counts 8,000 accounts; the overlap finding says many are the same order seen from different ends of the chain; and Margit Ekelund's one consolidated portal would collapse fourteen accounts into one.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board committee meets on Monday, 12 October at half past six, and the FY27 budget closes on 31 October. The Cuttack and Balasore offices shut from 17 to 21 October for Durga Puja and the Berhampur desk runs at half strength thereafter, so anything approved on Monday starts in November — by which time European buyers will have closed their Christmas order books and limit-hits will have fallen back to their February level.

The 2022 commitment holds the co-operative free tier open until 31 March 2028 and has already been paid for. The Series A of ₹34 crore, raised in January 2025, carries a board expectation of ₹15 crore ARR by 31 March 2027 against ₹9.20 crore today. Kalyani's full request is ₹1.72 crore a year. Rashmi's fresh notice and re-consent flow is costed at ₹18 lakh and six weeks of engineering, and the engineers are committed to EDPMS reconciliation until the end of November. Margit Ekelund wants her portal by 1 December.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does the trigger actually measure? Using Figure 1 and Exhibit 4, say what a limit-hit in June tells you about an account, and what it does not.
  2. Reconcile Exhibits 2 and 3. Which number should the board see, and how would you describe the difference without making the reps sound dishonest?
  3. Exhibit 5 splits the pilot at a pricing change nobody told the pilot about. What does that imply about treating a threshold as a property of customers?
  4. Exhibit 7 shows the score working; Exhibits 4 and 6 suggest it restates the sign-up segment and records Anubhav's own onboarding. How would you test which it is, and what would you stop doing to run that test?
  5. Whose interests does a qualification score serve here — the customer's, the rep's, the data team's, or the chief executive's story to investors? What would you change about rep pay before trusting this data?
  6. It is Monday morning. What do you do about the ₹1.72 crore, the consent notice and Margit Ekelund's portal — and what do you tell a board that has seen Exhibit 2 and believes the argument settled?

11. After midnight

At a quarter past one Debasmita wrote a single line at the top of her notes — what is the unit? — and sat looking at it. Outside, a generator started for the pandal lights. She could defend the score for twenty minutes on Monday, and calling everybody for ten. What she could not explain was why a company whose whole advantage was a buyer portal had spent a year learning to score suppliers.

Product-Led Sales: Letting the Product Tell You Who Is Ready to Buy

How usage data — not a lead form, not a conference badge scan — becomes the signal that tells a sales team exactly which accounts to call, and exactly when.

1. A Tuesday in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of September, Ananya Rao sat in a glass-walled conference room on the fourth floor of an HSR Layout office block, looking at a slide she had built the night before and did not enjoy showing. Ananya was the VP of Growth at Cobalt Metrics, a four-year-old company that sold a product-analytics and observability platform to engineering teams — the kind of tool a developer installs on a Tuesday afternoon without asking anyone's permission, watches dashboards populate by Thursday, and either loves or abandons within three weeks. Cobalt's self-serve funnel was, by the standards of Bengaluru SaaS in 2026, genuinely healthy: about 1,850 free signups a month, a website that ranked well for "error tracking for microservices," and a product that engineers actually recommended to each other on Slack. The problem was not signups. The problem was the fourteen account executives sitting one floor below, whose quota for the half-year had just been raised by 30 percent, and whose calendars were half full of outbound calls to companies that had never touched the product at all.

The numbers Ananya had pulled were blunt. Of the roughly 22,000 free signups Cobalt had accumulated over the previous eighteen months, only 640 had ever been contacted by a salesperson, and those 640 had been chosen the way most B2B software companies choose them: a signup used a corporate email domain with more than 200 employees on LinkedIn, so a sales-development representative added them to a sequence of three cold emails and two cold calls. Of those 640, 46 had converted to a paid contract — a 7.2 percent hit rate that the sales leader, Vikram Sethi, defended as "about what outbound always converts at." Meanwhile, sitting quietly inside Cobalt's own product database, unexamined by anyone in sales, were 210 free accounts where a customer had, in the last thirty days, invited six or more colleagues, connected a production data source, and built at least three dashboards — the exact behavioural fingerprint, it would later turn out, of a team that was already running the product as if it mattered to their job. Only 11 of those 210 had ever received a phone call. Two had converted anyway, on their own, without sales ever touching them; the other 198 sat untouched in a database, doing the one thing a product-led company cannot afford to let happen to its best accounts — nothing.

Ananya's board presentation was in nine days. She had to propose, with numbers rather than conviction, how Cobalt would close the gap between "usage says this account is ready" and "a salesperson knows to call it." That gap has a name in the growth literature, and getting it right is the difference between a sales team that burns quota chasing strangers and a sales team that spends its calls on people already halfway convinced. The name is product-led sales, and it rests on two more specific ideas — the product-qualified account and the product-qualified lead — that Ananya was about to have to explain, correctly, to a board that had heard the acronyms before but had never seen them built.

2. The Idea

Product-led sales (PLS) is a go-to-market motion in which usage data generated inside the product — not a form fill, not a trade-show badge scan, not a purchased list — is the primary signal a sales team uses to decide which accounts to pursue and when to pursue them. It sits downstream of two older ideas the reader has likely already met. Product-led growth (PLG), a term the venture firm OpenView Partners and its partner Blake Bartlett popularised around 2016, describes companies whose product itself — not a sales team — does the work of acquiring, converting and retaining users, typically through a free trial or freemium tier that lets a person experience value before anyone asks them for money. Sales-led growth, the older and still-dominant model in enterprise software, puts a human being at the centre of the buying journey from the first conversation onward. Product-led sales is the deliberate marriage of the two: let the product do the acquiring, as PLG prescribes, but instead of leaving every account to self-serve or churn silently, use what the product observes about each account's behaviour to decide which ones deserve a human salesperson's attention, and route that attention with precision instead of guesswork.

The two working units of this motion, refined and named by OpenView's growth team — particularly Kyle Poyar — over 2018 and 2019 as PLG matured from a curiosity into an investment thesis, are the product-qualified account (PQA) and the product-qualified lead (PQL). A PQA is an organisation whose aggregate usage pattern — number of active seats, breadth of features touched, depth of technical integration — crosses a threshold that historically correlates with becoming a paying, expanding customer. A PQL is a specific person inside that account whose individual behaviour — requesting an admin feature, inviting teammates, hitting a usage cap — marks them as the most useful person to talk to first. The distinction matters enormously in practice, and section five returns to it, but the sentence Ananya needed for her board, one she could say without sounding like she was reciting a vendor's blog post, was this: a product-qualified account is not a lead your marketing team found — it is a customer your product already half-sold, waiting for someone to notice.

3. How It Actually Works

The mechanics of a working PLS motion are less glamorous than the acronym suggests, and most of the difficulty lives in steps that practitioners describe as obvious and then quietly skip. The first step is instrumentation: someone has to decide, concretely, which product events are worth recording at all — not every click, but the ones with theoretical reason to predict commercial intent, such as inviting a teammate, connecting a data source, hitting a plan limit, or generating an API key. Cobalt Metrics, like most companies at this stage, already had an event-tracking pipeline for product-engineering purposes; the growth team's first real job was not building new plumbing but re-reading it with a commercial eye, which is a genuinely different exercise from reading it with a product-usability eye.

The second step is aggregation from the level of an individual user's clicks up to the level of an account's overall posture — a non-trivial data-engineering task, because a "seat," an "email address," and an "organisation" are three different objects that have to be reliably tied together, often across multiple domains, shared inboxes and free-tier signups that never stated a company name at all. The third step is scoring: converting a basket of raw signals into a single number or tier that a non-technical salesperson can act on without needing to interpret a scatterplot. The fourth step, routinely treated as an afterthought and just as routinely the reason these programmes fail, is threshold-setting and ownership — deciding, and writing down, exactly which score triggers a human touch, who is accountable for that number, and how often it gets revisited. The fifth step is routing: piping the qualified account into the CRM system the sales team already lives in, with enough context — which features, which seats, which trend — that the first outreach can reference something specific rather than opening with "I see you signed up for a free trial." The sixth and most neglected step is the feedback loop: recording what happened to every account sales did and did not call, and feeding the outcome — won, lost, ignored, converted anyway — back into the scoring model, because a model calibrated once in year one and never touched again slowly drifts away from the customer base it was built to describe.

Figure 1. The six steps of a product-led sales pipeline, from raw usage event to sales outreach, closing on itself through a feedback loop that most teams build last — or never.

Two of these steps deserve a sentence each, because they are the ones a newcomer most often assumes away. Aligning product and sales on a shared definition of "qualified" sounds administrative, but it is a genuine negotiation: a product manager tends to define quality in terms of technical depth — did the account integrate a real production data source — while a salesperson tends to define quality in terms of buying signals — did someone from finance or procurement show up. Both are legitimate and neither is sufficient alone, and Cobalt's early scoring model, built by an engineer without input from Vikram's sales team, had weighted technical depth so heavily that it kept flagging accounts run entirely by a single enthusiastic developer with no budget authority and no plan to ever ask for one.

4. A Worked Example, With the Arithmetic Shown

Cobalt's growth team eventually settled on a five-signal scoring rubric, each converted into a point band so that a salesperson could see, at a glance, why an account scored the way it did rather than trusting an opaque number. The rubric is shown below exactly as it went into Cobalt's internal wiki in the last week of that quarter.

SignalWhat it measuresPoint bands
Seat activation ratioActive users ÷ seats invited<20% = 0 · 20–40% = 10 · 40–70% = 18 · >70% = 25
Weekly-active-user trendWeek-over-week change in active seatsDeclining = 0 · Flat = 8 · Growing <20% = 14 · Growing ≥20% = 20
Dashboards builtNumber of saved dashboards or alerts created0 = 0 · 1–2 = 6 · 3–5 = 12 · 6+ = 15

5. The Nuances a Learner Must Become Aware Of

PQA and PQL answer different questions, and conflating them wastes both.

A PQA tells you which organisation to prioritise; a PQL tells you which individual inside that organisation to call first. Cobalt's early model produced only account-level scores and handed SDRs a company name with no named contact, which meant every outreach call opened by asking a receptionist-equivalent gatekeeper who used the product — an entirely avoidable friction that a proper PQL layer, tracking which individual generated the admin action or hit the usage cap, would have removed.

A high score is correlation with propensity, not proof of intent.

The scoring rubric was built by looking backward at accounts that eventually converted and asking which behaviours they shared before they did; it says nothing certain about any single new account, and Cobalt learned this the hard way when a university research lab scored 68 points purely by virtue of having many curious students poking at every feature, with zero budget and zero intention of ever paying.

It is a leading indicator of receptivity, not a substitute for qualification.

A PQA score tells a salesperson that a conversation is likely to be welcomed, not that the account has budget, authority, need and timeline. The old sales discipline of establishing those four things does not disappear because the product supplied the introduction; it simply starts from a warmer position.

Thresholds decay, and nobody notices until the sales team stops trusting the queue.

The 60-point threshold that worked when Cobalt's ideal customer was a 30-person startup engineering team began over-qualifying once the company moved upmarket toward 500-person logistics and fintech firms, whose usage patterns per seat looked structurally different; a model recalibrated once at launch and never revisited slowly stops matching the customer base it describes.

Heavy usage can mean a champion — or a person managing you out.

A support or customer-success team investigating a churn risk sometimes generates a usage spike that looks numerically identical to a genuinely expanding account — many logins, many dashboards, much activity — and a model with no way to distinguish "increasingly happy" from "increasingly worried" will route both cases the same way.

Data plumbing and consent are not someone else's problem.

Every signal in the rubric above is, in effect, personal and organisational data, and instrumenting it without a clear consent and retention policy creates real exposure under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act as much as under GDPR for accounts headquartered abroad; a growth team that treats this as a legal afterthought inherits the risk months later, usually during a customer's own security review.

A score cannot tell you who the economic buyer is.

Usage data describes what people do inside a product; it says almost nothing about who signs the purchase order, which is why a mature PLS motion always pairs the usage-based score with firmographic and technographic enrichment — company size, industry, existing tool stack — bought or scraped from outside the product entirely.

Premature human contact can slow the very motion it is meant to accelerate.

Self-serve buyers often convert faster and at higher margin when left alone; an SDR call that arrives too early can introduce friction, discounting expectations, or a multi-week procurement process onto a purchase that would otherwise have completed with a credit card in eleven minutes — a tension the next section returns to directly.

6. How the Picture Changes by Product and by Stage

In consumer products, product-led sales in the strict sense — a human salesperson calling an account — barely exists, because consumer average revenue per user rarely justifies a salesperson's time; what survives from the same underlying logic is lifecycle marketing, where a "PQL-like" signal, such as a user hitting a storage cap, triggers an in-app upgrade prompt or an email rather than a phone call. Calyx Notes, a consumer note-taking app with millions of free users, uses exactly this pattern: nobody at Calyx has ever called a free user, but their product triggers a targeted in-app nudge the moment someone exceeds 500 notes, because that behaviour predicts upgrade far better than any demographic data ever could. In B2B software — Cobalt Metrics's own world — PQA and PQL are close to the central nervous system of the entire growth motion, because contract values are high enough to justify a salesperson's hour and because the buying unit is genuinely a group of people rather than one individual, which is precisely why the account-level aggregation problem described in section three matters so much more here than anywhere else.

Marketplaces complicate the picture further because usage has to be scored on two sides of the same transaction independently. Cirrus Mandi, a business-to-business wholesale marketplace connecting small retailers to distributors, tracks a buyer-side PQA built from reorder frequency and basket growth, and an entirely separate seller-side PQA built from catalogue depth and response time to buyer enquiries — a seller who lists thousands of products but never replies to a query is not "qualified" in any sense that matters, no matter how large their catalogue looks on paper, and a marketplace that scores only one side of its network will systematically starve the other. Stage matters as much as product category: at an early-stage company, this scoring exercise is usually a spreadsheet a single growth PM updates by hand once a week, and the threshold is a defensible guess rather than a statistically fitted number — which is exactly the right level of rigour for the data volume available. At a company the size Cobalt was becoming, the same exercise moves into a dedicated RevOps function, the scoring model becomes a proper machine-learning propensity model retrained on a schedule, and the output lives natively inside the CRM the sales team already uses rather than in a spreadsheet anyone has to remember to check.

7. Common Mistakes

The first and most common mistake is weighting every signal in the model as though it carried equal predictive value, usually because it was easier to instrument than to validate. The symptom is an SDR team drowning in a queue of "qualified" accounts that convert no better than accounts picked at random; the underlying misunderstanding is treating instrumentation coverage as a proxy for commercial relevance, and the cheapest diagnostic is a simple one — pull the actual conversion rate by score band, and if the 90-to-100 band converts no better than the 60-to-70 band, at least one signal in the rubric is doing no real work and should be re-weighted or dropped.

The second mistake is calling too early, before an account's usage has stabilised into a genuine pattern. The symptom is a spike in cancellations or downgrades in the days immediately following a first sales call; the underlying misunderstanding is treating "crossed the threshold" as synonymous with "wants to talk to a human right now," when in truth many self-serve buyers actively prefer to complete a purchase without any human contact at all. The cheapest diagnostic is a simple experiment: hold out a random slice of newly qualified accounts for a three-to-five-day delay before outreach, and compare their eventual conversion rate and deal size against the group contacted immediately.

The third mistake is building the scoring model once and never closing the feedback loop described in section three. The symptom is a scoring queue that sales quietly stops trusting, working it half-heartedly or ignoring it altogether in favour of their own instincts; the underlying misunderstanding is assuming that a model, once validated, stays valid as the customer base and the product itself keep changing underneath it. The cheapest diagnostic is tracking two ratios every quarter — PQL-to-opportunity conversion and opportunity-to-closed-won rate — and treating any sustained decline in either as a mandatory trigger for retraining, not a mere data point to note in a deck.

The fourth mistake is confusing seats purchased with seats actually used, which sounds too obvious to be common and yet drives real churn. The symptom is a large account, seemingly healthy by contract value, that fails to renew; the underlying misunderstanding is reading commercial size as a proxy for product health when the two frequently diverge, especially in accounts bought top-down by a single executive sponsor who never drove adoption below them. The cheapest diagnostic is comparing licensed seats against weekly-active seats for every account above a chosen contract-value threshold, on a standing dashboard someone actually looks at before renewal conversations, not after.

8. What Good Looks Like

Eighteen months after that Tuesday board meeting, Cobalt Metrics ran a version of this motion that looked almost unglamorous in its discipline. A cross-functional group — one person each from product, sales operations and growth, calling itself the PQA council with a self-deprecating shrug about the name — met on the first Monday of every month to review exactly the two ratios named above: PQL-to-opportunity conversion, which had risen from 8 percent to 22 percent over that period, and opportunity-to-closed-won rate, which had held steady near 34 percent even as volume tripled. The scoring rubric itself had been revised three times, each revision documented with the specific evidence that prompted it — the seat-activation bands, for instance, were widened after the shift upmarket toward larger logistics and fintech customers changed what a "normal" activation ratio looked like for a 500-seat account. SDRs were given a mandatory three-day cooling window before contacting any newly qualified account below a certain deal-size threshold, a policy adopted directly from the delayed-outreach experiment described above, and above that threshold calls still went out same-day because the data showed larger accounts responded better to speed. None of this required exotic machine learning; it required treating the scoring model as a living artefact with an owner, a review cadence, and a documented history of why each number was what it was — the single habit, more than any particular formula, that separated the version of this motion that worked from the version that quietly rotted.

"The model isn't the hard part," Ananya told her board nine months later. "The hard part is remembering, every single quarter, that the model is only as good as the last time someone checked it against what actually happened."

9. What Ananya Decided

At that first board meeting, Ananya did not propose the full council-and-cadence system described above — that came later, earned through two quarters of visible failure and correction. What she proposed on that Tuesday was narrower and more defensible: build the five-signal scoring model exactly as shown in section four, set an initial threshold of 60 using the best available backward-looking data even though it was thin, route qualified accounts to a single pilot SDR rather than the whole team, and commit publicly to reviewing the model's actual conversion performance after ninety days rather than assuming it worked because it was live. She was explicit with the board about what the model could not yet do — it could not tell them who held budget authority inside a qualified account, and it would very likely misfire on interesting edge cases like the university research lab — and she framed the ninety-day review not as a formality but as the actual test of whether the idea deserved to survive contact with Cobalt's real customer base. The board approved it, not because the arithmetic in her deck was impressive, though it was, but because she had been honest about exactly where its edges lay.

What to learn next, and why: a natural next step from here is product-led growth into enterprise — the broader question of how a company built on frictionless self-serve motion learns to also close the six- and seven-figure contracts that self-serve alone rarely produces — and the case of how Asana built and staffed exactly this kind of seeding-and-selling motion as it scaled, which turns the abstractions in this page into one company's specific, occasionally uncomfortable, choices.

Two questions worth sitting with: First, in your own organisation, who currently owns the definition of "qualified" — and would product and sales actually give you the same answer if you asked them separately, in different rooms, today? Second, if your best customer's usage data had been visible to a salesperson on the day it first crossed whatever threshold matters, would that salesperson have known what to say — or would the call have opened with "I see you signed up for a free trial"?

Product-Led Sales at Depth

Why the useful signals are the ones a champion cannot send alone — and why the accounts that score highest are often the ones you should not call

This page assumes you already know what a product-qualified account is, how a scoring rubric is assembled from usage events, and why a feedback loop matters. It begins where that knowledge stops: with identity resolution, base rates, incrementality, capacity constraints, purpose limitation under Indian data-protection law, and the uncomfortable finding — replicated in every company that has bothered to run the experiment properly — that the best-scoring accounts frequently generate the least incremental revenue when a salesperson calls them.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On the morning of 4 February 2026, Meera Krishnan sat in a half-empty office on Senapati Bapat Road in Pune with a results table she had been dreading for six weeks. Meera ran growth at Jaladhi Cloud, a five-year-old infrastructure company that sold managed vector search and streaming ingestion to engineering teams on pure consumption pricing — no seats, no licences, a credit card and a rate limit. Jaladhi had ended 2025 at ₹86 crore of annualised revenue, growing 74 percent year on year, with 11,400 workspaces that had spent something in the trailing ninety days and a sales organisation of nine account executives and six sales-development representatives. By the standards of the Indian developer-tools cohort — the world that Postman and BrowserStack had shown was possible — Jaladhi was doing well.

The table in front of her said that roughly two-thirds of the revenue her sales team had been credited with over the previous two quarters would have arrived anyway. Eighteen months earlier Jaladhi had built exactly the kind of product-qualified-account programme that the literature prescribes: signals, weights, a threshold, a queue in the CRM, an owner, a monthly review. It had worked, on the numbers everyone looked at. Product-qualified leads converted to opportunity at 21 percent against 6 percent for cold outbound. Sales loved the queue. The board had been shown the chart twice.

Then, in August 2025, at the insistence of Tobias Lang — a data scientist Jaladhi had hired in Berlin, who had spent four years before that doing uplift modelling for a European retailer and who therefore found the whole exercise methodologically naive — the company had started randomly withholding a quarter of newly qualified accounts from any sales contact at all. No call, no email, no in-app nudge. Six months of that holdout now sat in the table on Meera's screen, and it said that in the highest-scoring band, where Jaladhi's best AEs spent most of their time, accounts that were called converted at 11.4 percent and accounts that were ignored converted at 10.0 percent. The sales team was, in that band, adding 1.4 percentage points and taking credit for 11.4.

Meera's decision was not whether the number was true — Tobias had pre-registered the design and she had checked the randomisation herself. Her decision was what to do with it in a company where the head of sales, Arjun Deshmukh, ran a commission plan that paid on closed-won revenue, where the CFO's productivity model credited sales with every rupee of a called account, and where killing outreach to the top band would look, on every dashboard the board had ever seen, like sales capacity going idle. Her board deck was due on 19 February.

Eleven days after Meera opened that table, on 9 February 2026, Dr Nandita Iyer faced a differently shaped version of the same problem in Hyderabad. Nandita was a physician who had stopped practising in 2018 and was now chief product officer at Jyotika Health Systems, which sold outpatient scheduling, lab ordering and e-prescription workflow to clinics and diagnostic chains, with records structured for the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's interoperability requirements. Jyotika had 3,100 tenants on a free single-practitioner tier and 640 paying accounts, median annual contract value ₹4.2 lakh, with a handful of multi-site chains between ₹40 lakh and ₹1.6 crore.

That morning a tenant called Jhelum Diagnostics Network — a twenty-six-centre pathology chain operating across Telangana and coastal Andhra — had, in eleven days, bound fourteen physical locations to a single tenant, created a three-level role hierarchy, configured the lab-instrument adapter, granted user-management rights to a second administrator, and run an audit-log export. On Jyotika's metadata-only scoring model, that combination had a historical 180-day conversion rate of 47 percent. It was the highest-scoring free tenant Jyotika had ever produced.

Nandita could not call them. Or rather, she could not call them without first resolving an argument that had begun the previous afternoon between Suresh Pillai, who ran enterprise sales and pointed out — correctly — that a chain of that size configuring audit-log exports was a chain preparing to run a procurement process, and Priya Menon, Jyotika's counsel and data-protection officer, who pointed out — also correctly — that the consent notice on the free tier enumerated "service operation and product improvement" as the purposes for which usage telemetry was processed, and said nothing whatever about commercial outreach. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, purpose limitation is not a formality you paper over afterwards. Re-consenting 3,100 tenants would take six to ten weeks and would visibly lose some of them. Not re-consenting meant watching the best account of the year run a tender Jyotika might not be invited to.

These two decisions — Meera's about incrementality, Nandita's about observability — are the two axes along which expertise in product-led sales actually lives. Everything else is bookkeeping.

2. The idea, precisely: a signalling problem, not a scoring problem

Product-led sales is usually defined as the use of in-product usage data to prioritise sales effort. That definition is true and nearly useless, because it describes the input and the output while saying nothing about the mechanism. A sharper definition, and the one this page will defend, is this: product-led sales is the practice of inferring an organisation's commercial intent from the costly, hard-to-imitate actions its members take inside a product, and then allocating a scarce and expensive human resource — a salesperson's hour — to the accounts where that inference is both confident and actionable. Three words in that sentence do the work. Costly, because free actions carry no information. Organisation, because you are selling to an entity, not a person. Scarce, because if sales capacity were unlimited the whole exercise would be unnecessary — you would simply call everyone.

The intellectual history is older and less Silicon Valley than the acronyms suggest. The direct branch runs from database marketing: the recency-frequency-monetary segmentation that catalogue retailers used from the 1960s onward, in which the best predictor of a future purchase turned out to be the pattern of past behaviour rather than any demographic descriptor. Marketing automation dragged the same logic into software with Eloqua in 1999 and Marketo in 2006, producing lead scoring built on email opens, webinar attendance and pricing-page visits. Product-led growth — the term popularised by OpenView Partners and Blake Bartlett around 2016, and the specific PQA and PQL vocabulary refined by Kyle Poyar and others over 2018 and 2019 — did not invent the scoring machinery. It changed the substrate: from behaviour observed about a prospect, at arm's length, to behaviour performed inside the thing being sold.

The deeper ancestor, and the one that explains why the substrate change mattered so much, is Michael Spence's 1973 work on market signalling. Spence's insight was that in a market with asymmetric information, the signals that separate types are the ones that are differentially costly to send. A claim anyone can make for free conveys nothing, because everyone makes it. A costly action conveys information precisely because the people for whom it is not worth the cost will not take it. Transpose this into software. A pricing-page visit costs nothing; anyone can emit it, including a competitor doing research and a student writing a term paper. Configuring SAML single sign-on costs a great deal: it requires a conversation with an IT department, a change request, an identity-provider administrator's time, and usually a security review. Almost nobody does it idly. The reason SSO configuration is a famously good PQA signal is not that it is technically related to buying. It is that it is expensive to fake, and expensive in a currency — other people's organisational attention — that only a real buying organisation possesses.

The through-line of this page. The quality of a product-led sales programme is determined almost entirely by how much of its score is built from signals that a single enthusiastic user cannot emit alone. Signals an individual can produce by themselves tell you about a person, and are the raw material of a product-qualified lead. Signals that require the co-operation of a second function — IT, finance, compliance, procurement, a second business unit — tell you about an organisation, and are the only honest raw material of a product-qualified account. Most failing programmes fail because they measure enthusiasm and call it intent.

This gives the PQA/PQL distinction a foundation that is more than taxonomic. It is not merely that a PQA is a company and a PQL is a person. It is that the two are built from structurally different classes of signal, and a team that scores both from the same event stream has not understood the difference. Jaladhi's original model, like most, summed everything into one number; the day Tobias Lang split it into "actions a solo developer could take in an afternoon" and "actions requiring someone else's budget or permission", the second sub-score alone outperformed the combined model on ninety-day conversion.

The schools, and the proposition each will and will not sign

Four positions are held by competent, experienced people, and they disagree in ways that cannot be dissolved by definition. The propensity school, which is the mainstream and the default of every CRM vendor, holds that the score should estimate the probability that an account converts, and that sales should work the queue from the top down. It will sign: "rank accounts by likelihood to buy, and spend the first rep-hour on the likeliest." It will not sign: "deliberately skip the highest-probability accounts." The incrementality school, imported largely by people with a background in causal inference or performance marketing, holds that probability of conversion is the wrong objective entirely, and that the score should estimate the change in conversion probability caused by contact. It will sign: "an account that will buy anyway should be routed to self-serve, not to an AE." It will not sign: "PQL conversion rate is a measure of programme health."

The heuristic school, associated with practitioners who have watched sophisticated models die of neglect, holds that transparency beats accuracy because a salesperson who cannot see why an account was flagged will not trust the flag, and an untrusted queue is worth nothing regardless of its AUC. It will sign: "a five-signal rubric a rep can read aloud beats a gradient-boosted model nobody can interrogate." It will not sign: "the model should be optimised for predictive performance." The self-serve primacy school, whose strongest historical evidence is Atlassian's long refusal to run an outbound sales team, holds that human contact is a cost and a friction that erodes the very margin structure product-led distribution exists to create. It will sign: "every account that requires a call represents a product or packaging failure we should fix rather than staff around." It will not sign: "a seven-figure enterprise agreement can be reached without a human being."

There is a fifth position that rarely writes blog posts but holds most of the world's enterprise revenue: the sales-primacy school, descended from BANT and its modern successors such as MEDDIC. It holds that usage tells you about receptivity and nothing about budget, authority, compelling event or procurement path, and that a PQA is therefore a superior list, not a qualification. It will sign: "PQA replaces the prospecting list; it does not replace qualification." It will not sign: "a high-usage account is a qualified pipeline opportunity."

3. Mechanics in depth: the six steps that are actually nine

The canonical pipeline — instrument, aggregate, score, threshold, route, learn — is a fair description of the visible work and a poor description of the hard work. Three of the steps hide sub-problems that consume more engineering and political effort than everything else combined.

3.2 Label definition, and the horizon nobody writes down

A propensity model predicts a label, and the label is a choice. Jaladhi's first model predicted "became a paying account", which in a consumption business every workspace technically does the moment it exceeds the free allowance. The model therefore learned to predict developers who would spend ₹800 a month, and it did so with impressive accuracy. The label was changed to "reached ₹25 lakh of annual committed contract value within 180 days of first spend", at which point the base rate collapsed from 34 percent to 1.8 percent and the model had to be rebuilt from scratch. The horizon matters as much as the event: a 90-day label trains a model that finds fast self-serve expansion, and a 365-day label trains a model that finds slow enterprise procurement, and these are different models that will rank the same population differently. A team that has not written its label and horizon on a whiteboard has not built a model; it has built a mood.

3.3 The scoring arithmetic, worked

Jaladhi's post-rebuild model is a logistic regression on six binary features, chosen over a gradient-boosted alternative that scored better on held-out AUC (0.81 against 0.77) because the coefficients could be printed on one line in the CRM and the sales team would therefore read them. The fitted form, with the label "₹25 lakh committed within 180 days":

log-odds = −4.10 + 1.05·(three or more distinct departments active) + 0.82·(spend growth above 40 percent week-on-week for two consecutive weeks) + 0.64·(production-grade authentication configured) + 0.47·(billing contact added, distinct from the technical signup) + 0.39·(support ticket referencing SLA, uptime or security) − 0.55·(single-developer workspace with no invitations in 60 days)

The intercept encodes the base rate: an account with no features at all sits at log-odds −4.10, which is a probability of 1/(1+e4.10) = 1.6 percent, closely matching the observed 1.8 percent population rate. Now take two real accounts from December 2025. Janpath Logistics, a Gurugram freight-visibility company, had three departments active, two weeks of 40-plus percent spend growth, production authentication configured, and a billing contact added by someone in finance. Its log-odds are −4.10 + 1.05 + 0.82 + 0.64 + 0.47 = −1.12, giving a probability of 1/(1+e1.12) = 1/(1+3.065) = 24.6 percent, roughly fifteen times base rate. Jarul Textiles, a Tiruppur exporter, had tripled its raw monthly spend over the same period — on paper the more exciting account — but the growth came from a single engineer running a historical backfill, with no invitations in sixty days and no configuration of any kind. Its log-odds are −4.10 + 0.82 − 0.55 = −3.83, a probability of 1/(1+e3.83) = 1/(1+46.06) = 2.1 percent. Raw consumption tripled; modelled intent barely moved. That divergence is the entire argument of section 2 expressed in two arithmetic lines, and it is the reason a consumption business must never let revenue growth serve as its own qualification signal.

Jaladhi's six SDRs can each carry about fifty-five live accounts and turn over roughly forty percent of that book monthly, which is 130 genuinely-worked new accounts per SDR per month, or 780 across the team — 2,340 per quarter against a population of 11,400.

First, quarterly capacity of 2,340 accounts is slightly more than two deciles, so the effective question is never "what is the threshold" but "where does decile 2 end", and the threshold is therefore a property of headcount, not of customers. When Jaladhi added two SDRs in March 2026, the correct threshold moved down even though nothing about the product or the market had changed — a point Arjun Deshmukh found genuinely counterintuitive and which cost two meetings to settle. Second, a three-times lift sounds modest and is in fact very good; teams that report twenty-times lift are almost always measuring on a population they have already filtered, which is the denominator problem in section 6.

4. Propensity is the wrong objective: the holdout, worked

Everything above estimates the probability that an account converts. Almost nothing above estimates the thing a business actually wants to know, which is whether calling the account changes whether it converts. These are different quantities, they are not monotonically related, and the difference between them is where most of the money in product-led sales is won or lost.

Formally, for account i, propensity is P(convert | account features) and uplift is P(convert | features, contacted) − P(convert | features, not contacted). Uplift cannot be estimated from observational data no matter how sophisticated the model, because the accounts a sales team chose to call differ systematically from the ones it did not, and the difference is exactly the thing you are trying to measure. The only honest instrument is a randomised holdout, which is why Tobias Lang insisted on one and why almost no company runs one: it requires deliberately not calling accounts you believe will buy, every quarter, forever, and telling the CFO that this is a feature.

The four-way taxonomy that uplift practitioners use is worth naming because it changes how a sales leader reads a queue. Sure things convert whether or not you call; effort spent on them is waste dressed as success. Persuadables convert only if you call; they are the entire economic justification of the function. 5. When the idea applies, when it does not, and the seams

The conditions under which product-led sales earns its overhead can be stated as four testable claims, and it is worth applying each to both protagonists rather than nodding at them in the abstract.

Claim one: the product must be usable to a point of genuine value before money changes hands. If a prospect cannot reach meaningful usage without a contract, there is no usage to observe, and PLS reduces to lead scoring on marketing signals. Jaladhi passes emphatically — a developer reaches production value in an afternoon. Jyotika passes only partially: a single doctor can run a free clinic workspace, but a twenty-six-centre chain cannot meaningfully pilot without an implementation, so Jyotika observes small-scale usage and must extrapolate to enterprise intent, which is a different and more fragile inference.

Claim two: the observable behaviour must be causally connected to the buying decision, not merely correlated with organisational size. The test is whether the signal survives controlling for company size. Half the rubrics in circulation fail it: they flag large companies, which convert more because they are large, and the model has learned nothing the firmographic data did not already contain. Jaladhi ran this test in October 2025 by adding employee count as a covariate; three of the original nine signals lost all significance and were dropped. Jyotika's signals — role-hierarchy depth, audit-log export, multi-site binding — survive the test well, because they are configuration acts rather than volume measures.

Claim three: the average contract value must exceed the fully-loaded cost of the human intervention by a wide margin, at the incremental rather than the attributed level. Jaladhi clears it comfortably on the aggregate (₹99,000 against ₹31 lakh) and fails it in two of five bands. Jyotika's median ₹4.2 lakh ACV against an SDR sequence cost of roughly ₹1,100 and an implementation-led sales cycle averaging eleven weeks of an AE's partial attention is much tighter; for its small-clinic segment the honest answer is that no human should ever call, and Jyotika's correct motion there is in-product and lifecycle, not sales.

Claim four: the usage must be legible to you at all. This is the condition the literature almost never states because in the American SaaS context it is nearly always satisfied. It is not satisfied in Nandita Iyer's world, and the ways in which it fails are instructive: legal purpose limitation, contractual prohibitions in enterprise agreements on content-level analytics, on-premise and virtual-private-cloud deployments where the vendor sees nothing, and — increasingly — customers who deliberately deploy through a gateway that strips telemetry.

The situations where PLS is actively misleading rather than merely unhelpful deserve naming. A product bought top-down by a mandate — compliance tooling, statutory reporting, anything a regulator obliges a firm to buy — will show poor usage in accounts with high purchase intent and excellent usage in accounts that will never expand. A product with a strongly seasonal or event-driven use pattern generates qualification spikes that are artefacts of the calendar. And a product in the middle of a pricing change generates a beautiful spike in limit-hitting behaviour that reflects the new limits rather than any change in customer intent — Jaladhi qualified 340 accounts in a single week in June 2025 for exactly this reason, and its SDRs spent a fortnight calling people who were annoyed rather than interested.

Hard edge cases

Multi-product. Once a company sells two products, "the account is qualified" ceases to be a well-formed statement; the question is which product's sales team is qualified for it, and the answer is usually contested because compensation depends on it. The mature handling is a per-product PQA with an explicit arbitration rule — highest-uplift product wins, not highest-ACV product — plus a suppression window preventing two teams contacting the same buyer inside thirty days. What companies actually do, overwhelmingly, is let whichever team's system writes to the CRM first take the account, which is a race condition masquerading as a policy.

Two-sided markets. Jhoomar Bazaar, a B2B wholesale marketplace matching small-town retailers with apparel distributors, discovered in 2025 that its supply-side PQA was actively harmful. Distributors with deep catalogues and rising order volume scored highest and were sold premium placement; but the binding constraint on the marketplace was buyer trust, and the highest-volume distributors were also the ones with the worst fulfilment reliability, so selling them more distribution degraded the network. The correct signal on a two-sided platform is not "who is growing" but "who is growing in a way that improves the other side's experience", which means the PQA must include a cross-side quality term. Jhoomar's revised supply-side score multiplies catalogue and volume by a fulfilment factor, and roughly a third of the previously top-scoring distributors dropped out of the queue entirely.

Regulated products. Jyotika's constraint turned out, unexpectedly, to improve its model. Denied access to clinical content, the team was forced to build entirely from administrative and compliance metadata: how many locations are bound to a tenant, how deep the role hierarchy goes, whether user-management rights have been delegated, whether a retention policy has been set, whether an audit-log export has been run. Every one of those is, in the language of section 2, a high-cost organisational signal — it requires someone with institutional authority to act. A clinical-content model would have measured how much doctors liked the software. The metadata model measures whether an institution is organising itself around it. The constraint pushed Jyotika above the signalling frontier by force.

Hardware plus software. Jaitra Instruments sells industrial energy meters with a cloud analytics layer and sells them through a distributor network across Gujarat and Maharashtra. Its telemetry is excellent — it knows exactly how many meters are live, how often dashboards are opened, whether alarm thresholds have been configured. Its problem is that the commercial relationship belongs to the distributor, so a qualified account cannot be called by Jaitra without cutting across the channel partner who sold it. Jaitra's working answer is to push the PQA to the partner rather than to its own sales team, along with the specific evidence, and to accept a slower and lossier conversion in exchange for not detonating the channel. This is the general shape of the answer wherever you do not own the customer relationship, and it is the case the PLS literature almost entirely ignores.

AI-native products. Three things break at once. Consumption is no longer a clean proxy for value, because an agent can emit enormous usage on behalf of one human. Cost of goods is variable and account-specific, so high usage can be unprofitable usage. And the usage curve is far noisier — a single evaluation run or a backfill can look like an enterprise rollout for seventy-two hours. Section 8 works through a company that learned all three the expensive way.
