6. Ten things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Costliness, not frequency, is what makes a signal informative. The competent practitioner builds a rubric out of whatever is well instrumented, which in most companies means page views, session counts and logins, because those were instrumented first for product analytics. The expert reads a rubric and asks, of each line, "how much of somebody else's authority did this action consume?" The tell-tale sign of the amateur version is a rubric in which the highest-weighted signal is a volume measure. The obvious reading — that more usage means more interest — is wrong because volume is emitted by the enthusiasm of individuals, and enthusiasm is abundant and cheap. Organisational authority is scarce and expensive, which is precisely why spending it is informative.

Propensity and uplift come apart, and the divergence is largest exactly where you are spending most. The competent practitioner optimises the model's ability to predict conversion. The expert knows that the accounts a model is most confident about are disproportionately accounts that would have converted regardless, because the same features that make conversion likely also make it likely without help. The tell-tale sign is a programme whose PQL-to-opportunity rate is rising every quarter while total new-logo revenue is flat: the model is getting better at finding people who were already coming. The obvious reading — that a higher conversion rate in the queue means a better queue — is wrong because conversion rate in the queue is not a causal quantity and cannot be improved past the point where you are simply selecting the inevitable.

The denominator is contaminated, and the model gets more confident as it gets more wrong. Outcomes are observed only for accounts someone chose to call. The model is retrained on those outcomes. It therefore learns the preferences of last year's sales team rather than the structure of the market, and each retraining tightens the loop. The tell-tale sign is a validation metric that improves monotonically across retrainings while the pipeline does not. The expert's defence is the same holdout that measures uplift, doing double duty as an unbiased sample of what happens to uncalled accounts; the competent practitioner treats the holdout as a measurement cost rather than as training data, which is a waste of the most expensive data the company generates.

The informative quantity is usually a second derivative, and usually about breadth rather than depth. Level tells you how big an account is, which you already knew. Rate of change tells you something. Change in the breadth of who is using — a second department, a second geography, a second job function — tells you the most, because breadth is the observable shadow of an internal decision to standardise. The tell-tale sign of the immature model is that the top of the queue is always the largest companies. The obvious reading — that big accounts are good accounts — is wrong not because it is false but because it is uninformative: you did not need telemetry to find large companies, and a model that rediscovers firmographics has added nothing.

Negative signals are systematically underweighted, and most rubrics cannot subtract at all. Almost every scoring model in circulation is a sum of non-negative terms. But an admin removing seats, a failed integration retried nine times, a support ticket about billing disputes, a sudden drop in a previously-active department — each of these is strongly predictive, and predictive in the direction that should stop a call. Jaladhi's single negative term (dormant single-developer workspace, coefficient −0.55) did more to clean the top of its queue than any positive term added that year. The tell-tale sign is a rubric with no minus sign anywhere in it. The obvious reading — that scoring should measure engagement — is wrong because what you want to measure is the probability of a good outcome, and evidence against is as informative as evidence for.

Latency dominates accuracy over the ranges most companies operate in. A model with an AUC of 0.74 acting within two hours beats a model with an AUC of 0.83 acting in five days, by a margin that Table 4 makes concrete. The tell-tale sign is a team that has spent two quarters on feature engineering and still runs a nightly batch into a queue reviewed weekly. The obvious reading — that the model is the intellectual core of the system and therefore the right place to invest — is wrong because the model's output decays; a qualifying event is a window into a moment of organisational attention, and organisational attention moves on.

The threshold is a property of your headcount, not of your customers. A PQA threshold is the point at which the marginal account is worth a rep-hour, and the value of a rep-hour is set by how many rep-hours exist. Hire two SDRs and the correct threshold falls; lose four and it rises. The tell-tale sign is a threshold expressed as a round number (60, 70, 80) that nobody can date and that has survived two changes in team size. The obvious reading — that the threshold expresses what "qualified" means — is wrong because qualification is not a property of the account; it is a property of the match between the account and your capacity to act on it.

Once reps can see the signals, the signals stop being signals. This is Goodhart's law in its purest commercial form. An AE who knows that "billing contact added" is worth 0.47 will ask a friendly champion to add a billing contact so the account enters the programme and the AE gets air cover to work it. The tell-tale sign is a sudden spike in one signal concentrated in a small number of reps' accounts, usually late in a quarter. The obvious reading — that transparency with the sales team is good — is right and is also the mechanism of the problem; the expert's answer is not opacity but a small set of signals that are expensive for a rep to induce, plus quarterly monitoring of signal distribution by rep.

Usage identifies the champion; it almost never identifies the buyer, and in India the distance between them is larger. Indian enterprise procurement is more often finance-led and more often annualised around the April fiscal year than its American equivalent, and the practitioner who mistakes a delighted engineering manager for a buying decision will spend a quarter learning this. The tell-tale sign is a pipeline full of opportunities with a single named contact. The obvious reading — that the enthusiastic user will bring the buyer along — is wrong often enough to be dangerous; the champion's enthusiasm is a necessary condition and a poor predictor of the procurement path, which is why the sales-primacy school in section 2 keeps winning arguments it is not supposed to win.

Silence is a signal, and the same machine that finds buyers finds churn. An account whose usage stops is emitting information at least as valuable as one whose usage starts, and it is usually more urgent, because renewal dates are fixed and attention is scarcest just before them. The tell-tale sign of the immature programme is a PQA system wired only to new-business sales, with customer success running an entirely separate health score on the same event stream with different definitions. The obvious reading — that acquisition and retention are different functions with different needs — is organisationally true and analytically false; they are the same inference problem with the sign flipped, and running two uncoordinated models on one event stream guarantees that both will be wrong in different ways.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Jaladhi Cloud: the reallocation that looked like a productivity decline

Between March and June 2026 Jaladhi held total SDR capacity constant at 2,340 sequences for the quarter and changed only the allocation rule: the top band was capped at 150 sequences (down from roughly 420 at the equivalent run-rate), the 70–84 band was worked exhaustively at 1,180, the 55–69 band took 710, and everything below 55 was removed from the queue entirely and routed to an automated in-product sequence instead. The permanent holdout was reduced from 25 percent to 12 percent, which Tobias calculated was still sufficient to detect a 2-percentage-point effect at the band level within two quarters.

Reported results, as the sales dashboard showed them: wins credited to sales fell from 150 to 121, a 19 percent decline, and the closely-watched PQL-to-opportunity conversion rate fell from 21 percent to 16 percent. Estimated results, as the holdout showed them: incremental wins rose from 42 to 61, a 45 percent increase, worth roughly ₹5.9 crore of additional committed revenue against unchanged cost. Meera spent more time in the quarter explaining the first pair of numbers than she had spent building the entire programme. The decisive artefact was not the analysis; it was a change to Arjun's team's compensation plan, agreed in April, under which 20 percent of SDR variable pay moved onto incremental-win estimates at the band level rather than raw meetings booked. Without that change, every individual in the sales organisation would have been correctly incentivised to undo the reallocation.

8.2 Jyotika Health Systems: a model built from what it was not allowed to see

Jyotika's metadata PQA, live since June 2025, scores nine configuration signals and no content signals whatsoever. Over the following twelve months, 112 of 3,100 free tenants crossed the threshold. Those 112 converted to paid at 18.8 percent within 180 days (21 accounts); the 2,988 below threshold converted at 0.8 percent (24 accounts). The lift is 23-fold, far above anything Jaladhi achieved, for two reasons: the underlying base rate is lower, and — the more interesting reason — every signal in the model is above the signalling frontier by construction, because the only data the lawyers permitted was administrative configuration data, and administrative configuration is precisely what institutions do and individuals do not.

Jyotika has never run a randomised holdout, and Nandita is candid that she does not know how much of the 18.8 percent is incremental. Her rough internal estimate, from the nine of twenty-one accounts that had already begun a procurement conversation through other channels before the call, is that the true incremental figure is closer to twelve accounts, implying an uplift of roughly eleven percentage points. She regards this as a guess and says so in board meetings, which is more intellectual honesty than most of the field manages.

8.3 Jugalbandi Labs: the failure, and what recovery actually cost

Jugalbandi Labs, a Bengaluru company selling an agent-orchestration platform priced per thousand agent-runs, built a PQA in late 2025 on the most obvious available signal: run volume and its growth rate. The model worked, in the sense that it predicted conversion to annual committed contracts with a top-decile lift of 4.1 times. Over the first half of 2026 the sales team closed 34 annual commitments from the queue: ₹24.9 crore at list, discounted an average 22 percent to ₹19.4 crore of committed revenue. The board was delighted, and the company's Series B was raised partly on that chart.

The problem, which the head of growth Kabir Anand surfaced in July 2026 after a finance analyst asked an awkward question about gross margin by cohort, was that inference cost varied enormously by account — from 8 percent to 71 percent gross margin depending on model tier, average context length and retry rate — and run volume was negatively correlated with margin. The accounts that emitted the most runs were the ones doing high-retry, long-context, frequently-failing work on the most expensive model tier. The queue had been, in effect, a detector for the company's worst-unit-economics customers. Inference cost against those 34 contracts came to ₹20.7 crore, giving a gross margin of −6.7 percent before a further ₹2.1 crore of solutions-engineering and support cost. The committed contracts ran twelve months and could not be repriced.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of catching them late

The first and most expensive failure mode is qualifying on proxies for size rather than intent. Its early warning is that the top of the queue is always the same twenty logos. The diagnostic question that catches it: if I add employee count as a covariate, do my signals retain significance? Caught early it costs a week of re-fitting. Caught late — and it is usually caught at the two-year mark, when someone finally compares the model's recommendations against a list generated purely from firmographics — it costs the credibility of the entire function, because the honest finding is that telemetry added nothing.

The second is the silent schema break. Its early warning is a signal whose weekly volume drops by more than forty percent without a product release that would explain it. The diagnostic question: does every signal in the model have a volume alert with an owner who is paged? Caught within a week it costs nothing. Caught after a quarter, as happened at Jaladhi in early 2025 when a renamed authentication event silently zeroed the 0.64 coefficient, it costs a quarter of misrouted capacity and, worse, a retraining cycle that learns from contaminated data and bakes the error in.

The third is attribution inflation, in which the programme is credited with conversions it did not cause. Its early warning is a PQL-to-opportunity rate that improves every quarter while net-new revenue does not. The diagnostic question: what is our best estimate of what would have happened to these accounts if we had done nothing, and how did we obtain it? If the answer contains no randomisation, the estimate does not exist. Caught late, this failure mode does something subtler than waste money: it causes the company to over-hire sales capacity against a return that was never real, and the correction usually arrives as a layoff.

The fourth is calling too early into a self-serve motion, creating sleeping dogs. Early warning: an increase in deals that stall in "procurement" for more than sixty days among accounts whose contract value would not normally require procurement. Diagnostic question: for accounts below our median deal size, is contacted conversion actually higher than uncontacted conversion? Caught late, the cost is paid in cycle time across the whole small-account cohort, and it is nearly invisible because nobody counts the credit-card purchases that did not happen.

The fifth is signal gaming by the sales team. Early warning: a signal's distribution becomes concentrated in a small number of reps' accounts, particularly in the final three weeks of a quarter. Diagnostic question: if I plot each signal's incidence by owning rep, is any rep an outlier by more than two standard deviations? Caught late, the model degrades in a way that looks like market change, and the team spends two quarters re-fitting a model whose training labels are corrupt.

The sixth is the expansion misroute: treating a new workspace inside an existing customer as a new prospect. Early warning is customer-success managers hearing from their accounts that "someone from your sales team called us about signing up". Diagnostic question: does the account hierarchy resolve child workspaces to paying parents before scoring, and is that suppression tested? Caught late, it costs specific named relationships, and in Indian enterprise sales — where a single unhappy CIO speaks to peers at three other firms — the reputational cost is disproportionate to the number of incidents.

The seventh is governance drift on the data itself. Early warning: a customer's security questionnaire asks a question about telemetry use that nobody in the company can answer the same way twice. Diagnostic question: does our consent notice enumerate commercial outreach as a purpose, and can we produce the record? Caught late — which under the DPDP Act means caught by the Data Protection Board rather than by you — the cost is not merely financial; it is the requirement to stop processing, which switches off the programme entirely and without notice. This is the failure mode Nandita Iyer was trying to avoid on 9 February.

There is a fifth disagreement that is less discussed and more consequential, and it concerns the unit of analysis. One camp holds that the account is the only coherent unit, because organisations buy software. The other holds that the person is the only observable unit, because organisations do not click buttons. The practical form of the argument is whether a company should build a PQA and derive contacts from it, or build PQLs and roll them up. Jyotika's experience, where the account-level configuration signals dramatically outperform individual-level engagement signals, supports the first. Jaladhi's experience, where the single best predictor turned out to be a named individual in finance adding a billing contact, supports the second. Nobody has a general answer, and the honest position is that the right unit depends on whether your product's buying decision is made by an institution reorganising itself around a tool or by a person deciding to spend a budget they already control.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic builds a rubric, sets a threshold, ships a queue and reports a conversion rate. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in five observable ways.

They ask what the label is before they ask what the signals are, and they write the horizon down. They insist on an addressable denominator, so that every rate they quote is over accounts they could actually have contacted rather than over raw signups, and they are unembarrassed that this makes their numbers look worse. They defend the holdout in every budget conversation, and they have a prepared answer for the CFO who asks why the company is deliberately leaving revenue uncollected — the answer being that the holdout is the only instrument that distinguishes revenue the company earned from revenue it merely witnessed. They treat latency as a first-class engineering commitment with an SLA, not as an operational detail, because they have seen Table 4. And they audit signals for organisational cost rather than for statistical significance alone, because they know that a signal which is significant but cheap will be gamed, drift, or turn out to be a proxy for size.

There is a sixth behaviour that is harder to describe and separates the very best. They hold the score loosely. They know that the model is a device for allocating attention under scarcity, not a description of the world, and that its correct threshold moves when headcount moves, its correct objective moves when the company's constraint moves from growth to margin, and its correct signals move when the product changes. They can say, out loud and in front of a board, "this number was right last year and is wrong now, and here is what changed" — which is a sentence that requires having written down, at the time, why the number was what it was.

12. What Meera and Nandita decided

Meera Krishnan presented the holdout results to Jaladhi's board on 19 February 2026, and she made a choice that experienced operators will recognise as the politically correct one and methodologists will find timid: she led with the measurement change, not the motion change. Her proposal was that Jaladhi adopt incremental wins as the reported measure of sales-sourced pipeline from Q1 onward, restate the prior two quarters on the new basis so that the board saw the discontinuity once rather than wondering about it for a year, and only then — in the following quarter, with the new measure already established — change the allocation rule. Her reasoning was that if she changed the motion first, the reported numbers would fall, and she would be defending a reallocation with a measure nobody had yet agreed to. She also committed to a permanent 12 percent holdout written into the operating plan rather than the analytics backlog, on the grounds that anything in the backlog eventually gets deprioritised by someone who does not know why it is there. Arjun Deshmukh supported the proposal after the compensation change was agreed, and not before, which Meera considered entirely reasonable.

Nandita Iyer took the narrower path on 12 February 2026, three days after the Jhelum Diagnostics score crossed. On Priya Menon's advice she did not use the tenant's clinical telemetry. She did make the call, on a basis Priya was prepared to defend: the specific signals used — number of locations bound to the tenant, delegation of user-management rights, and the audit-log export — are attributes of the account's own configuration, initiated by the named administrator in the course of administering a contract Jyotika was party to, and arguably not personal data being processed for a new purpose at all. She instructed the sales team in writing that no clinical-usage figure was to be referenced on the call, and she began the consent re-papering in parallel, accepting the six-to-ten-week timeline. She was explicit with her own board that the narrow basis was a judgement call rather than a settled legal position, and that if the Data Protection Board's guidance developed unfavourably, Jyotika would have to rebuild its qualification model on consented data or on no data at all. Jhelum Diagnostics signed a ₹62 lakh annual agreement on 30 April 2026. Nandita's view, stated to Suresh Pillai afterwards, was that they had got the right answer through a process she would not want to rely on twice.

Discussion questions

  1. Meera changed the measure before changing the motion. Arjun would have preferred the reverse — change the allocation quietly, let the incremental results accumulate, and present both together in six months. Which sequencing is right, and what does your answer imply about how much you believe a sales organisation will tolerate a measurement change it did not ask for?
  2. Jyotika's constraint — no access to clinical content — produced a better-performing model than Jaladhi's unconstrained access did. Is this a coincidence of these two companies, or is there a general argument that constrained telemetry forces teams above the signalling frontier? If the latter, what would you deliberately refuse to look at in a product where you were permitted to look at everything?
  3. Jugalbandi's failure was not a modelling failure; the model predicted conversion accurately. It was a failure to specify the objective, and the correction required a weekly data flow from finance into growth that most companies do not have. Whose job was it, at Jugalbandi, to notice — and what structural arrangement would have made it somebody's job before ₹6 crore had been spent?

13. Going deeper

  • Product-led growth — the distribution model that makes any of this possible. Without a product a stranger can reach value in, there is no behaviour to observe; revisit it for the packaging and free-tier design decisions that determine which signals you will ever be able to see.
  • Sales-led growth — the qualification discipline that product data does not replace. The sales-primacy school of section 2 keeps winning arguments precisely because BANT-descended frameworks encode things telemetry cannot see; knowing that tradition well is what lets you referee the argument.
  • Case: Seeding and Selling Asana — a worked account of one company building this motion at scale, including the staffing and compensation questions that section 8 shows are the binding constraint rather than the analytics.
  • Product-led growth into enterprise — the direct sequel: what changes when the deals get large, procurement appears, and the champion is three levels below the buyer. This is where the signalling-frontier argument does the most work.
  • What a GTM strategy is — the frame that decides whether PLS is your motion at all. PLS is one allocation rule inside a strategy; adopting it without the strategy produces a well-run queue pointed at the wrong market.
  • Your first 100 users — the stage before any of this is estimable. Read it for what to do when n is too small for a model and the founder is the scoring function.
  • Channels: paid, owned, earned — where the accounts in your queue come from in the first place. Channel mix changes the composition of your signals: paid-acquired accounts emit different early behaviour from referral-acquired ones, and a model that ignores channel will confound the two.
  • Inbound vs outbound — the other side of Figure 3. You cannot set a PQA threshold correctly without knowing the marginal return of the outbound alternative, which makes this topic a prerequisite rather than a complement.
  • Launch planning and launch mistakes — pricing and packaging changes reset every signal distribution you have fitted. Read it for the discipline of coordinating a launch with the teams whose models it will silently invalidate.
  • Crossing the chasm — Geoffrey Moore's argument explains why the accounts that self-serve enthusiastically early are systematically unlike the accounts that will constitute the mainstream market, and therefore why a model trained on early adopters mis-ranks the market you actually need to win.
